\chapter{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
For Software Architecture Part 2 we chose to add the third party services (M1) and availability (Av2).
This means we had to add a way for utilizing the data from third party fitness tracking services to improve the clinical models accuracy and make sure that when communication between the patient gateway and the pms (Patient Monitoring System) backend fails there is an alternative way of contacting the patient or the service operator.
To accomplish this we zoom in on the prediction pipeline and the communication channel between the pms and the patient gateway.


\chapter{QAS Decisions}\label{sec:decisions}



\section{Qual1: Include third party lifestyle tracker data in clinical model computations (M1)}
\subsection*{Key Decisions}
To get  third party data into our system without breaking anything that already works or slowing down our main prediction engine, we made the following four key architectural decisions:
\begin{adlist}
	\item  We introduced an abstract parent component called \nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceThirdPartyAPIs}. This acts as a reusable blueprint that child components (like \texttt{StravaAPI} and \texttt{GoogleFitAPI}) implement. It hides all the API details from the rest of our app.

	\item  We included a \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformPatientDataStorage} in the pms specifically for storing third party patient data.

	\item We included a seperate storage \nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceTokenStorage} for sensitive tokens.

  \item  We placed a component, \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformHISManager}, between our platform and the hospital information system.
\end{adlist}

\subsection*{Architectural Decision 1:
ThirdPartyApi's}

For contacting third party services we added the \nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceThirdPartyAPIs} component. This serves as an abstract parent blueprint implemented by the googlefit and strava children. Working in this way allows new third party services to be implemented by implementing the blueprint component. This ensures that they can be added in less than \texttt{2 weeks}.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
Strategy Pattern and Polymorphism

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{Interface Stability:} The development speed of adding a new service is highly sensitive to how well-designed the parent class is. If the abstract blueprint is too bloated or changes frequently, it will cause ripple effects across all child classes, breaking our 2-week implementation guarantee.
	\item \textbf{Credential Exposure Risk:} Because these sub-components handle active network connections to external servers, they are a primary target for security leaks. We must strictly ensure that third-party authentication tokens are never logged or exposed during API handshakes; they must be securely fetched on-demand and kept isolated from public layers.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This blueprint relies directly on our decision to establish a local database layer (\nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformPatientDataStorage}). This allows us to check if we already got earlier data from the third party which we can use rather than fetching the same data again.
\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
This layout makes the system slightly larger and introduces some initial structural overhead because developers have to implement a parent-child structure rather than just writing a direct script. However, this trade-off is highly justified: we trade a small amount of extra upfront code complexity for long-term modifiability.
Including the \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformPatientDataStorage} also reduces latency of the prediction process because we don't always have to contact the third party servers.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Single component.}
An alternative could be having a single, large component to contact all third party apis. However this would lead to a cluttered class once more and more third party apis are added. This parent child structure also gives a clear blueprint for developers to implement which is important for adding new services in less than 2 weeks.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Architectural Decision 2:
	Patient DataStorage }

This is our local database \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformPatientDataStorage} for storing the patient thirdparty data and the patient's status. Those cannot be stored in the hospital information system.

Instead of our clinical prediction engines making real-time, synchronous network calls to external api's like Strava or Google Fit whenever a risk evaluation job runs, the system queries this local storage. If a third-party service experiences an outage or a latency spike, the prediction pipeline continues uninterrupted by falling back onto the last known valid data cached here.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
Single responsiblity and Data Caching

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{Cache Freshness and Outdated Predictions:} The clinical value of using lifestyle metrics is highly sensitive to how frequently our background tasks update this database. If the update intervals are spaced too far apart, the clinical job engine will process stale tracker data, which could reduce the accuracy gains expected by the clinical model.
	\item \textbf{Performance:} Since this repository is queried every time a new clinical job creator process kicks off, its access latency must remain minimal. If query execution times degrade under high system loads, it will propagate directly into the overall duration of the patient risk estimation timeline.
\end{itemize}


\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This decision works hand-in-hand with the abstract plugin blueprints (\nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceThirdPartyAPIs}]). The concrete child integration plugins handle the external API polling logic and continuously push fresh data packages directly into this storage component. the clinical job creator checks the recentness of the available rows in this cache databas. It can then, depending on the recentness of the available data poll for new data from the ThirdPartyApi as seen in \nameref{diag:Interaction:Thirdpartypolling}.
If the patient is not using a third party service or when the third party service or patient database is unavailable, the clinical job creator will continue without the third party data.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
By adding a dedicated local storage layer, we introduce extra data management overhead, structural database footprint, and complexity. However, this trade-off is incredibly beneficial: we completely decouple our core clinical pipeline from unreliable third-party network links, ensuring high system availability and predictable estimation performance under all operational conditions.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Storing in the hospital information system (his).}
This would be the best option if we could edit the his to store this data as it moves the security responsibility to the hospital, however it is not possible as we cannot control what can be stored in the his as it depends on the serviced hospital.

\paragraph{no patient DataStorage}
It would be possible to implement this without a patient datastorage, this would mean that on every prediction job we have to fetch all the patient data from the third party services. However adding the datastorage offloads work of the third parties, it reduces latency and with a implementation deadline of 3 months we should have more than enough time to implement this extension.

\subsection*{Architectural Decision 3: Token Storage}

To handle the highly sensitive nature of user authentication tokens, we decided to separate them entirely from other storage systems by introducing a dedicated \nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceTokenStorage} component. This serves as a standalone, tightly locked cryptographic vault specifically for storing tokens to poll third-party platforms like Google Fit and Strava.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
Information Encapsulation, Security Tiering

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{Encryption Latency vs. Throughput:} Because tokens are cryptographically secured at rest, reading them requires decryption operations. The retrieval mechanism is highly sensitive to encryption configuration choices; if decryption handshakes take too long, it could choke background synchronization workers when they attempt mass data polls for multiple users simultaneously.
	\item \textbf{Access Vector Control:} The entire point of this vault is security isolation. The configuration must be locked down so that only the background data ingestion layers can query it. Connecting unnecessary components to this database instantly breaks our security tiering tactic and compromises user credentials.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This database directly supports the polymorphic plugin layer (\nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceThirdPartyAPIs}). Before a child plugin can initiate an external network handshake to download patient metrics, it must first check out the valid active token from this storage component. Conversely, it has zero relation to the primary hospital systems or standard sensor processing lines, keeping our security boundary clean.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
Splitting our data into two separate databases (\nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformPatientDataStorage} for data and \nameref{mod:ComponentsThirdPartyServiceTokenStorage} for credentials) naturally makes our architecture slightly more complex and means we have to manage multiple databases. However, this trade-off is absolutely necessary: it lets us apply heavy, compliant encryption and strict role-based access rules directly to the sensitive tokens without destroying the database access speeds required to read massive volumes of data.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Alternative: Putting Everything into a Single Database.}
We considered keeping things simple by storing third-party tokens and fitness tracker data side-by-side in the same database table under a single schema. While this would keep our system layout smaller and simplify data queries, we rejected it because it violates the principle of security tiering. Forcing our clinical analytics engine to continuously read from a table holding raw, decrypted authentication keys would create a massive security vulnerability and make compliance audits incredibly difficult.


\subsection*{Architectural Decision 4:
	HIS Manager}

We placed a dedicatedabstraction, the \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformHISManager}, between our platform and the external Hospital Information System (HIS). This component acts as an abstraction layer that handles all communication with the hospital's health API, translating our internal system requests into the data formats required by the specific hospital backend.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
Database Abstraction layer

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{API Request Overhead:} This component must be optimized to handle database operations on the HIS as efficiently as possible, utilizing batch requests or lightweight lookups.
	\item \textbf{Data Minimization:} Because the HIS contains highly regulated and sensitive electronic health records (EHR), the HIS Manager must follow the principle of least privilege. It should expose only the minimal necessary endpoints to other internal components to prevent unauthorized internal data leakage.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
The HIS Manager provides a centralized data gateway for the patient gateway endpoint (as seen in \nameref{diag:Interaction:Incomingsensordata}), the clinical job creator, and the risk estimator combiner. They route their hospital data lookups exclusively through this manager instead of making scattered, direct health API calls. This fits with our goal of localized modifiability; if the hospital changes its underlying database schema or API protocol, this is the only component in our entire architecture that needs to be modified.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
Introducing an extra abstraction layer adds a small amount of initial code complexity and a tiny performance hit due to data translation at runtime. However, this trade-off is well worth it. Skipping the HIS Manager would force multiple internal components to manage their own authentication methods and direct connections to the health API. That would create a massive security risk by spreading our API credentials across the system and would make adapting our platform to a new hospital incredibly difficult.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Polymorphism.}
Just like we did for the third-party api's, we considered implementing a parent-child structure where a generic blueprint is inherited by specific subclasses for every hospital deployment. However, since our platform is currently integrated with only a single hospital, building an entire object-oriented polymorphic hierarchy right now would add unnecessary complexity without providing immediate value. If the system scales to support multiple hospitals simultaneously in the future, transitioning this component to a polymorphic blueprint will be straightforward because the data access logic is already safely isolated inside this single component.

\section{Qual2: Communication between patient gateways and PMS backend (Av2)}
In order to satisfy availability by handling fault-tolerance in the primary communication channel, we made the following architectural decisions:
\subsection*{Key Decisions}
\begin{adlist}
	\item Implementation of \nameref{mod:ComponentsPatientGatewayAppSyncManager} and a \nameref{mod:ComponentsPatientGatewayAppBuffer} module on the \nameref{comp:ComponentsPatientGatewayApp} to handle a continuous 24-hour network failure gracefully.
	\item Implementation of a server-side \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformCronjob} component that acts as a periodic timer loop, auditing liveness states tracking at the \nameref{comp:ComponentsPatientGatewayEndpoint} to autonomously identify missing transmissions.
	\item Implementation of an external \nameref{comp:ComponentsSMSgateway} to route emergency notifications over standard GSM signaling when IP-based transport links are non-operational.
\end{adlist}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Architectural Decision 1:  SyncManager and Buffer}
To maintain operational continuity and detect communication failure on the app-side, we introduced SyncManager and a buffer module, which represent a circular buffer, directly within the internal infrastructure of the Patient Gateway App component. Rather than allowing network exceptions to cascade into the data collection threads of the application, the SyncManager acts as an interceptor for all outbound data transmissions.

Instead of crashing or blocking the data-collection routines, the transaction exception is routed to the SyncManager. The SyncManager immediately transitions the gateway application into a local degraded mode.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
\begin{itemize}
	\item By utilizing exponential back-off, we prevent device battery depletion and backend server storming during network reconnection phases.
	\item The buffer has a capacity for 24 hours of sensor data at the configured transmission rate. When the buffer is full, the oldest entry is overwritten by the newest. Only the timestamp of the overwritten packet is logged prior to overwriting, preserving auditability without requiring retention of the full sensor payload. This policy prioritizes recency over completeness, since the most recent sensor data is most clinically relevant for risk estimation when the connection is restored. The data loss for outages exceeding 24 hours is considered acceptable given the Av2 requirement explicitly limits the storage guarantee to 24 hours.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{enumerate}
	\item The availability of cardiovascular data during a prolonged outage is highly sensitive to mobile storage limits. Because our degraded mode relies entirely on the smartphone's local memory to buffer up to 24 hours of sensor data, allocating a buffer size that is too small will result in the oldest data being permanently overwritten and lost before the network is restored.
	\item While SyncManager is responsible for entering degrading mode and enforcing notifications of emergency notifs, we cannot make sure the SMS gateway is contacted when the patients phone has died.
	\item System performance and the throughput guarantees established in P2 are directly sensitive to the reconnection sync rate. When the network is finally restored and the SyncManager flushes its buffered data to the backend, an overly aggressive sync rate without proper batch sizing and backoff intervals could cause a fleet of reconnecting gateways to flood the backend, instantly forcing the RiskEstimationScheduler into overload mode.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This decision establishes the foundation for the application's client-side resilience and connects directly to both the backend Cronjob (AD2) and the external SMS Gateway (AD3). When the SyncManager detects a network failure, it switches to degraded mode silently without attempting to send an offline alert to the server. Because of this quiet client-side handling, the backend must rely entirely on the Cronjob to notice that the gateway has stopped transmitting. During this downtime, the SyncManager is responsible for continuously evaluating incoming sensor data and pushing any emergency alerts to the SMS interface. Finally, when the network is restored, the SyncManager pushes its buffered data back to the Patient Gateway Endpoint. This automatically updates the backend's \texttt{last seen} timestamps, allowing the Cronjob to clear the failure alert naturally without any manual resets from the telemedicine operators.


\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
\paragraph{Availability over modifiability}
To achieve higher availability and fault-tolerance, the SyncManager and buffer introduce complexity of the gateway app. It creates tighter coupling between data acquisition modules and transport layers, which ultimately reduces the system's long-term modifiability.
\paragraph{Monitorability over performance}
To satisy the autonomous failure detection, the backend must execute continous checks on liveness states of the gateways. This might introduce a steady performance cost in terms of CPU cycles, database query load, and resource consumption on the backend server.
\paragraph{Availability over safety}
We acknowledge full data recovery cannot be met when patiens phone dies, and therefor focus on prevention and proper report of lost timeslot of data.
The trade-off is completely acceptable because it strictly honors the 24-hour retention mandate while protecting device performance boundaries.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Drop new data instead of old data.}
During the design of the local buffer, we considered an alternative capacity management strategy where the system would simply stop accepting new sensor data once the 24-hour storage limit was reached, effectively dropping the newest readings. We ultimately rejected this approach because it directly conflicts with the clinical priorities of a patient monitoring service. In cardiovascular risk assessment, a patient's most recent physiological state is significantly more relevant for immediate medical decision-making than day-old historical data. By choosing to overwrite the oldest data instead, we ensure that when the gateway finally restores its connection, the backend receives the most up-to-date 24-hour snapshot of the patient's health, allowing the clinical models to generate a much safer and more accurate current risk estimation.


% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Architectural Decision 2: Adding the cronjob component}

The integration of a decoupled, server-side \hyperref[diag:Component:Primarydiagramoftheclientserverview]{\texttt{Cronjob}} component addresses the fundamental architectural challenge of isolating incoming data stream logic from orchestration and health-monitoring overhead. The \texttt{Cronjob} operates as an independent background daemon, which keeps a countdown for every patient's data.

By calculating the delta between the current system clock and the expected data-arrival interval of each active patient profile, the \texttt{Cronjob} can autonomously flag communication problems without introducing overhead to the data ingestion pipeline. To preserve high modifiability and strictly adhere to the Single Responsibility Principle, the \texttt{Cronjob} remains entirely separated of downstream notification policies. Once a failure state is declared, it hands off a structured exception event to the central \texttt{AlertManager}, which dynamically resolves the stakeholder routing logic.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
\begin{itemize}
	\item Utilizing existing, periodic scheduled payloads as connection validation (implicit heartbeats), optimizing client-side battery life and conserving restricted cellular bandwidth.
	\item The \hyperref[diag:Interaction:av2CommunicationchannelbetweenPMSandPGgoesdownDetectionbytimeoutBackend]{AlertManager} applies differentiated service levels by routing alerts through the AlertPush interface without queuing or batching, ensuring notification latency is bounded by detection time alone rather than queue depth. High-risk alerts are dispatched first, satisfying the 2/5/10-minute delivery windows by risk class.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item The scalability of this liveness tracking mechanism is highly sensitive to whether the execution is single-threaded or concurrent. While auditing a few hundred pilot patients is trivial, scaling to thousands of patients with a single-threaded loop will cause the execution time to grow, eventually causing the system's detection latency to drift past the required 5-minute deadline.
	\item The detection latency required by the Av2 scenario is entirely sensitive to the polling frequency and timeout threshold of the backend Cronjob. If this tracking loop runs too infrequently, the system will fail to detect missing transmissions within the strict \textit{expected time + 5 minutes} deadline, while running it too frequently will needlessly burn backend CPU resources.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This decision establishes a structural dependency on the data contract provided by the \texttt{Patient Gateway Endpoint} and coordinates directly with the downstream routing interfaces of the \texttt{AlertManager}. When an offline gateway restores its link and flushes its \texttt{buffer} using an exponential back-off chunking strategy, the endpoint's timestamp index is updated transparently. This allows the \texttt{Cronjob} execution cycle to reset the client's connectivity flag automatically.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
\paragraph{Availability over performance}
Introducing a multi-tiered pipeline (\texttt{Cronjob}, \texttt{Endpoint Ledger}, \texttt{AlertManager}) requires a higher structural overhead and more internal interface specifications than simply embedding connection timeouts inside the active network adapters.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Active Peer-to-Peer Polling from Backend to Client.}
An alternative approach considered was forcing the backend servers to actively broadcast periodic application-layer ping queries to every registered smartphone gateway at 60-second intervals to verify connection health. This alternative was rejected because active background radio polling rapidly drains the edge device's battery, violating the core user experience constraint of low physical invasiveness in the patient's day-to-day life, and scales poorly due to the compounding financial and bandwidth costs of continuous cell-tower polling.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Architectural Decision 3: Adding external SMS gateway}
To ensure critical health events are reported even during complete IP network outages, we integrated an external SMS gateway into the architecture. When the SyncManager detects a degraded network state but identifies a life-threatening anomaly (such as an emergency notification per UC3), it bypasses the standard PatientDataPush interface. Instead, it leverages the SMSinterface to transmit a highly compressed emergency payload over standard cellular GSM networks. This guarantees a secondary, out-of-band communication route for the most critical system alerts, ensuring patient safety is not entirely dependent on internet connectivity.

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{Active redundancy (Communication):} Deploying a secondary, independent physical communication medium (GSM) to back up the primary medium (IP/Wi-Fi/4G data).
	\item \textbf{Graceful degradation:} Reducing the emergency payload to its absolute bare minimum (dropping rich historical sensor graphs and metadata) to fit within the strict data constraints of an SMS message.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item The performance and safety of emergency notifications (UC3) are deeply sensitive to third-party API latency. Because the architecture delegates these critical alerts to an external SMSgateway, the end-to-end delivery time is dictated by the telecom provider's SLA, meaning any unexpected downtime or degradation on their end directly delays the hospital's emergency response.
	\item The cost and reliability of this fallback mechanism are highly sensitive to the strictness of the trigger condition used to activate it. A threshold that is too sensitive could result in costly, redundant SMS messages during minor network jitters, whereas a condition that is too loose will dangerously delay real emergency alerts.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This decision relies directly on the SyncManager (AD1) to act as the trigger mechanism. Because the standard IP communication channel is offline, the SMS gateway depends entirely on the client-side gateway app to perform the initial health triage and pass the highly compressed emergency payload to the SMSinterface.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
\textbf{Cost and Bandwidth vs. Safety:} Utilizing an SMS gateway introduces a per-message financial cost and severely restricts the payload size compared to standard IP traffic. By dropping the rich historical sensor graphs and metadata to fit within an SMS, we trade data completeness for the absolute guarantee that a life-threatening alert reaches the hospital. This perfectly aligns with the system's core priority: immediate patient safety always supersedes data granularity during a network crisis.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Open Wi-Fi / Mesh Network Hopping:}
We considered programming the gateway app to aggressively scan for and connect to nearby open Wi-Fi networks or use Bluetooth mesh networking to find an alternate route to the internet. This was rejected due to severe security and privacy vulnerabilities. Additionally, continuous radio scanning would rapidly deplete the device's remaining battery, worsening the availability problem.

\chapter{Other decisions}\label{sec:otherdecisions}

\subsection*{1. Manual Token-Entry User Interface on the Patient App}
We decided to implement a minimal user interface directly on the patient app where users can manually input or paste their third-party service authentication tokens.
\paragraph{Context and Justification:}
Integrating a full, native SDK or OAuth redirection flow directly inside the smartphone application (e.g., launching in-app browsers, handling complex redirect deep-links, and managing tokens locally on the device) would significantly increase development time. By opting for a simple configuration screen where the patient inputs their generated token, we cleanly separate the mobile client from the third-party platforms. The app transmits this text string to our backend server, which handles the actual integration. This design choice guarantees that we can extend and deploy the app changes in less than 1 month.

\subsection*{2. Notification Routing via the Alert Manager}
When communication failures or system anomalies are detected, the system offloads the notifications to a dedicated component: the \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformAlertManager}.

\paragraph{Context and Justification:}
To maintain high modifiability and adhere strictly to the Single Responsibility Principle, network detection components (like the cronjob) should not know how or who to notify when a failure occurs. Instead, once a failure state is declared, a structured exception event is handed off to the \nameref{comp:ComponentseHealthPlatformAlertManager}. This component resolves the alert. Centralizing this logic ensures that notification rules and thresholds can be modified or updated over time without requiring any redeployments or changes to our core endpoints.

\subsection*{3.. Architectural Infrastructure Decision: Patient and Operator Gateway Endpoints}

We established centralized entry and exit points for all remote communication via the \nameref{comp:ComponentsPatientGatewayEndpoint} and an \nameref{comp:ComponentsOperatorGatewayEndpoint}. These components act as traffic controllers separating our core backend layers from external clients—specifically the patients' smartphone gateways and remote service operators (such as doctors, nurses, and maintenance engineers).

\subsubsection*{Employed tactics and patterns}
Gateway Pattern, Single Responsibility, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).

\subsubsection*{Sensitivity points}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \textbf{Strict Least-Privilege Routing:} These endpoints are highly sensitive security boundaries. They must only map to the exact internal components required to fulfill their specific role workflows. Allowing an endpoint to connect to an unnecessary backend service risks letting a user cross boundaries and access restricted health information.
	\item \textbf{Single Point of Failure for Network Health:} Since all traffic flows through these points, any crash here completely cuts off backend visibility, making it a critical focus area for availability monitoring.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Relation to other architectural decisions}
This centralized layout directly supports our availability routing logic for scenario Av2. When communication drops or a patient gateway goes offline, having a single communication gateway allows our auditing components (like the server-side cronjobs and alert managers) to track connection drops in one consolidated ledger rather than having to scan scattered application logs.

\subsubsection*{Trade-off justification}
By funneling all external incoming and outgoing traffic through dedicated gateway components, we introduce an extra network hop and a potential system bottleneck. However, this trade-off is completely justified: it drastically reduces code duplication for common network tasks (such as connection retries, timeout strategies, and fallback behaviors) and gives our security team an isolated, easy-to-audit boundary to safeguard incoming data.

\subsubsection*{Considered alternatives}
\paragraph{Alternative: Direct Component-to-User Communication.}
We considered allowing every individual backend component to contact patient devices or operators directly whenever they had an update. We rejected this because it scatters communication logic across the entire system. If a network outage occurs, troubleshooting connectivity issues would become a nightmare, and implementing consistent security controls or global retry behavior would result in massive code duplication.

\paragraph{Alternative: Task-Specific Communication Gateways.}
Another option was to create multiple smaller gateways split by specific tasks (e.g., one for sensor data transfers, one for emergency alerts, and one for account settings). While this provides slightly better isolation, we rejected it because it splits our error-handling logic into too many places, making it harder to diagnose network failures quickly.
